description: Elegant Clarkia or Mountain Garland is a slender California native annual reaching 1-3 feet, producing delicate pink to purple flowers with distinctively clawed petals that give it exceptional refinement. Native to grassy slopes and woodland edges throughout California's foothills and mountains, it thrives in well-drained soils with minimal water. An excellent self-seeding annual for the naturalistic garden, it combines beautifully with other native annuals and perennials.
history_text_short: Elegant clarkia (also called mountain garland) is endemic to California. A distinctive spring-blooming annual with four-petaled flowers on slender wands whose petals have narrow "claws" (stalks) supporting rounded blades above — like tiny dancing figures. Widely grown from seed in California-native wildflower meadow plantings.
history_text_long:
Clarkia unguiculata is endemic to California — found essentially nowhere else in the world — growing in oak woodlands, chaparral openings, roadside slopes, and grassland edges across most of the state below 1500 meters elevation, from the North Coast Ranges south through the Sierra Nevada foothills and the Transverse and Peninsular Ranges. The species epithet "unguiculata" means "with small claws" and refers to the distinctive petal form: each of the four flower petals has a narrow stalk-like basal "claw" supporting a broader terminal blade, creating the effect of four tiny dancers balanced on tip-toe with arms spread. This distinctive flower form gives the common name "elegant clarkia" and "mountain garland." Flowers are typically pink, lavender, or purple, sometimes with darker markings, on slender 30-90 cm wands blooming in late spring to early summer.

The species is an important model organism in plant evolutionary biology, particularly in the study of speciation and mating-system evolution; University of California and Stanford University research programs have used Clarkia species extensively as a model system for understanding how new plant species arise through selfing versus outcrossing differences. Widely planted from seed in California-native wildflower meadow plantings as a colorful late-spring element, readily reseeding for subsequent years in appropriate dry-summer conditions. An important model organism in evolutionary biology, studied for decades by Verne Grant at the Rancho Santa Ana Botanic Garden.

Research on Clarkia species helped establish our understanding of plant speciation and hybridization in California's flora. The species is named for William Clark and classified elegantly by Lindley in 1830.
name_origin: 'Unguiculata' means 'clawed' in Latin, referring to the long narrow claw at the base of each petal.

uses_list.text: Spidery pink flowers feed native solitary bees
Slender wands mix into cottage bouquets

symbolism_list.description: refined clawed petals with exceptional elegance
intricate flower form rewards close inspection

symbolism_story: Elegant Clarkia can symbolize grace through its slender clawed petals, each blossom resembling a small dancer caught mid-step. Closer inspection reveals an intricate delicacy, fringed petals and finely poised stamens that reward the gardener who kneels to look. In the western American wildflower tradition, clarkia is the quietly refined companion, an annual that asks the eye to slow down and to find its delight in details easy to miss from a path.

description: Silver Torch Cactus is a striking columnar cactus from Bolivia and Argentina, forming clumps of slender silvery-white spined columns reaching 6-10 feet tall. Densely covered in fine white spines that give it a glowing silvery appearance, mature plants produce horizontal tubular deep-red flowers that never fully open—pollinated by hummingbirds in their native range. A dramatic specimen for desert landscapes from California to Arizona, and a popular collector cactus.
history_text_short: Silver torch cactus is a Bolivian high-Andean species. Heese described it as Cereus strausii in 1907 honoring German cactophile Leopold Strauss; Backeberg transferred to Cleistocactus in 1934. Forms clumping columns 1-3 meters tall densely covered in white bristles, producing deep carmine-red tubular flowers.
history_text_long:
Cleistocactus strausii, silver torch cactus, is a columnar cactus native to high-altitude slopes of the Andes in Bolivia and northern Argentina at 1800-3000 meters elevation. German horticulturist Emil Heese described it as Cereus strausii in 1907, honoring fellow German cactus enthusiast Leopold Strauss. German botanist Curt Backeberg transferred the species to Cleistocactus in 1934.

The genus name Cleistocactus (from Greek kleistos = closed) refers to the characteristic that flowers barely open at their tips. Plants form clumping columnar cacti with slender 5-10 cm diameter green stems reaching 1-3 meters tall, densely covered in white woolly bristle-like spines giving the appearance of fuzzy silver torches. In summer mature stems produce distinctive 8-9 cm long tubular deep carmine-red flowers horizontally oriented along the upper stem, adapted for hummingbird pollination, with only the tips opening to expose the anthers.

One of the most recognizable columnar cacti in cultivation and reasonably cold-tolerant down to short periods below freezing. Described in 1893 by Karl Schumann and named for German botanist Ludwig Strauss. A popular Hollywood-era ornamental cactus that defined many mid-century desert garden designs in the American Southwest.
name_origin: 'Cleistocactus' from Greek 'kleistos' (closed) for the never-opening flowers; 'strausii' honors Ludwig Strauss.

symbolism_story: The silver torch cactus is high-altitude endurance made visible, surviving thin air, brutal sun, and freezing nights in the Bolivian Andes with a stoic upright pillar form. Its brilliance is quieter — a coat of fine white spines that catches desert sunlight and turns each column into a silvery candle. Few cacti combine such severe habitat and such gentle, almost angelic, surface texture.

description: Alpine Clematis is a dainty deciduous climber reaching 6-10 feet, native to the mountain forests of Europe and Asia. In spring it bears nodding bell-shaped flowers in shades of blue, violet, pink, or white, followed by silky seed heads. Early-flowering and cold-hardy, it thrives in cooler US climates including the Northeast and Pacific Northwest and does not require the heavy pruning of summer-flowering types.
history_text_short: Alpine clematis is native to mountains of Europe and northern Asia. Miller described it as Atragene alpina in 1768, transferred to Clematis by P. Miller. Nodding blue-violet bell-shaped flowers open in spring on the previous year's wood. One of the easiest, hardiest, and most refined clematis for small gardens and cool climates.
history_text_long:
Clematis alpina is native to the mountains of central and eastern Europe (Alps, Carpathians, Balkans) and northern Asia. Scottish botanist Philip Miller first described it as Atragene alpina in 1768 in the Gardeners Dictionary; later taxonomists transferred it to Clematis. The epithet alpina reflects its high-mountain habitat.

Unlike the large-flowered hybrid clematis familiar to most gardeners, C. alpina belongs to the Atragene section—characterized by nodding bell-shaped to lantern-like flowers 3-5 cm long, with four violet-blue petaloid sepals surrounding a central boss of smaller white staminodes. Flowering occurs in April-May on the previous year's growth (group 1 pruning), so no hard cutting back is needed. The 2-3 meter vine is easy, forgiving, and extremely cold-hardy (to zone 3), thriving in conditions that defeat many of its showier Asian relatives.

Cultivars 'Pamela Jackman', 'Frances Rivis', 'Pink Flamingo' (pink), 'White Columbine', 'Ruby', and 'Willy' have been selected. Silvery seedheads extend interest into winter. Native to the Alps and mountain ranges of Europe and Asia, cultivated since at least the 16th century. Adapted superbly to cool US mountain and northern gardens.
name_origin: 'Alpina' refers to its alpine mountain habitat.

symbolism_story: Alpine Clematis carries the refined beauty of high places, its nodding bell flowers a quiet emblem of mountain grace. Native to the cool slopes of central European peaks, its early bloom signals renewal as winter at last gives way. To plant this clematis is to bring a piece of alpine spring into the lowland garden — a delicate climber whose dangling violet bells whisper that the long cold has truly ended.

description: Armand Clematis is a vigorous evergreen climber reaching 15-25 feet, producing abundant clusters of fragrant starry white flowers in early spring against glossy leathery dark green leaves. Native to central and western China, it is one of the few evergreen clematis and a showstopping vine for Southern and Pacific coast US gardens. A single plant in full bloom can perfume an entire garden.
history_text_short: Armand's clematis is native to central and southern China and northern Myanmar. Franchet described it in 1885, naming it for Père Armand David, the French missionary-naturalist who collected it. One of the few evergreen clematis, its powerfully fragrant white star flowers in early spring have made it a mainstay of mild-winter pergolas.
history_text_long:
Clematis armandii occurs naturally in central and southern China (Sichuan, Yunnan, Hubei, Guizhou, Guangxi) and northern Myanmar. French botanist Adrien René Franchet formally described the species in 1885, honoring Père Armand David (1826-1900), the pioneering French Lazarist missionary and naturalist who collected extensively in China and for whom the Pere David's deer, giant panda (David first documented it for Western science), and numerous plants are named. Ernest Henry Wilson introduced the species to British gardens in 1900.

Unlike most clematis, which are deciduous, C. armandii is evergreen with thick, leathery, lanceolate dark green leaves on vigorous vines to 6-10 meters. In March-April it produces masses of 4-6 cm pure white star-shaped flowers with a powerful sweet vanilla-almond fragrance that can perfume an entire garden.

Hardy only to about zone 7, it is a signature vine of mild-winter garden regions—the Pacific Northwest, Atlantic coast of Britain, Mediterranean Europe, and milder Southeast US. Cultivars 'Apple Blossom' (pink-flushed), 'Snowdrift', and 'Little White Charm' are popular.
name_origin: The common name highlights its green coloring. 'Armandii' honors Armand David (1826-1900), discoverer of many Chinese plants including the giant panda.

Paired with exuberance, it covers fences and pergolas in such dense flower that a structure can vanish beneath it. It is a vine for those who want spring announced not in whispers but in cascading, fragrant proclamations.

description: Clematis montana, the mountain clematis, is a vigorous, fast-growing climbing vine that covers fences and walls with masses of small, four-petaled white or pink flowers in late spring. Native to the Himalayas and central China, it can grow 10+ meters and produces such abundant bloom that the foliage nearly disappears. The vanilla-scented cultivar 'Elizabeth' with soft pink flowers is one of the most popular garden clematis. Unlike large-flowered clematis, it requires minimal pruning — just tidy up after flowering. It is one of the easiest and most rewarding climbing plants.
history_text_short: Mountain clematis was collected in the western Himalaya by British plant hunter Lady Amherst in 1831 and introduced to British gardens, where its spring cascade of pink and white flowers made it one of the most widely grown large-flowered climbers of the 20th century.
history_text_long:
Clematis montana is native to the Himalaya from Afghanistan through Nepal, Bhutan, and into western China. It was introduced to Britain in 1831 by Lady Sarah Amherst (wife of the British Governor-General of India), one of the pioneering European woman botanists in South Asia. The species became a foundation of English garden climbers, and the pink-flowered form C. montana var. rubens was introduced from western China by Ernest Wilson in 1900.

Its combination of vigorous growth, mass spring flowering, and ability to cover ugly structures made it a staple of British, French, and American gardens throughout the 20th century. Unlike the summer-blooming large-flowered Clematis hybrids descended from C. lanuginosa, C. montana flowers on previous year's wood, requiring only post-bloom pruning. Modern scented cultivars like "Elizabeth" extend its appeal.

Ernest 'Chinese' Wilson, the legendary plant hunter for Veitch Nursery, collected the pink-flowered var. rubens in China's Hubei province in 1900, adding the pink palette that dominates cultivation today. The genus Clematis contains about 380 species — the name comes from Greek 'klema' (vine tendril). Clematis montana is the fastest-growing of all clematis species, capable of adding 3+ meters per year. In its native Himalayan habitat, it climbs forest margins at elevations of 1,500–4,000 meters.
name_origin: Clematis from Greek 'klema' (vine or vine branch). Montana means 'of the mountains,' for its Himalayan origin.

symbolism_story: Himalayan Clematis embodies ingenuity, finding its way up trellis, tree, or wall through the patient twining of leaf stalks rather than tendrils, a quiet feat of botanical problem-solving. It covers structures in cascading spring blooms, transforming the unremarkable into the celebrated. It is often read as a flower of clever ascent, the climber who reaches the top not through force but through the inventive use of what most plants overlook.

description: Sweet Autumn Clematis is a vigorous deciduous climber reaching 15-30 feet that covers itself in small fragrant creamy-white flowers in late summer and early fall, creating drifts of starry blooms over fences and trellises. The honey-almond fragrance attracts pollinators while feathery seed heads extend the display into winter. Self-seeds easily and is considered invasive in parts of the eastern US, so cultivars with sterile seeds are preferred.
history_text_short: Clematis terniflora occurs naturally in Japan, Korea, Taiwan, and eastern China. Swiss botanist Augustin Pyramus de Candolle described the species in 1818. The epithet terniflora means three-flowered in reference to groups of three flowers on side branches.
history_text_long:
Clematis terniflora occurs naturally in Japan, Korea, Taiwan, and eastern China. Swiss botanist Augustin Pyramus de Candolle described the species in 1818. The epithet terniflora means three-flowered in reference to groups of three flowers on side branches.

The species was long confused with the similar-looking C. paniculata (a New Zealand native, now Clematis paniculata J.F.Gmel.) and C. maximowicziana, and American gardens mostly grow true C. terniflora. It is an enormously vigorous deciduous vine to 10+ meters, producing in late August-September a spectacular smother of creamy-white four-petaled star-shaped flowers 2-3 cm across, densely packed and emitting a powerful honey-vanilla scent.

Silvery fluffy seedheads follow, attractive well into winter. Introduced to North America in the 19th century, the species has thrived beyond anticipation and is now classified as invasive across the eastern US (especially Pennsylvania to Georgia), smothering native vegetation along roadsides and forest edges. Native alternatives include the less-vigorous Clematis virginiana (virgin's bower). Introduced from Japan to the US in the 1860s, it became a favorite Victorian garden vine for fall bloom. Listed as invasive in parts of the Mid-Atlantic and Southeast US where it escapes to cover native vegetation. Gardeners are encouraged to deadhead before seeds ripen.
name_origin: 'Terniflora' means three-flowered, referring to clustered blossoms.

description: Virgin's Bower is an eastern North American native deciduous vine reaching 10-20 feet, producing masses of small fragrant white flowers in late summer followed by attractive feathery seed heads called 'old man's beard'. Found in moist woodlands and stream banks across the eastern and central US, it supports native pollinators and provides habitat value. A vigorous but manageable native alternative to the invasive Sweet Autumn Clematis.
history_text_short: Virgin's bower is native to eastern North America. Linnaeus described it in 1753. The common name references the curly silver-white fluffy seedheads remaining after bloom. A native alternative to the invasive C. terniflora, it supports native pollinators and is an important host for the Large Lace Border moth.
history_text_long:
Clematis virginiana is native to eastern and central North America from Nova Scotia south through Florida and west to Manitoba, Kansas, Louisiana, and Texas, typically along woodland edges, streams, and fencerows. Linnaeus described the species in Species Plantarum (1753) from Virginia material, giving it the common name virgin's bower—the bower part refers to a sheltered arbor, and the virgin is thought to reference Elizabeth I (the Virgin Queen) for whom Virginia itself was named. The 3-5 meter vine produces panicles of small (2 cm) four-petaled cream-white flowers in late summer (August-September) followed by the feathery silvery-white seedheads that persist into winter and give the species its name.

While less visually overwhelming than the invasive Asian C. terniflora, it is a valuable native substitute, serving as a host plant for the Large Lace Border moth (Scopula limboundata) and providing late-season nectar for native bees and butterflies. Unlike the non-native C. terniflora it is dioecious—male and female flowers on separate plants. A widespread native vine beloved by colonial American gardeners.

Called 'Devil's Darning Needles' in folk tradition. Native Americans used it medicinally for nerve pain. Now promoted as a native substitute for the invasive Asian Sweet Autumn Clematis.
name_origin: 'Virginiana' refers to its range including Virginia, though it extends far wider across the eastern US.

That reserve gave it the Victorian meaning of virgin modesty — beauty that does not announce itself. As a native of wild thickets and stream edges, it carries the spirit of woodland places where grace is something stumbled upon rather than staged.

description: Clematis viticella, the Italian clematis, produces an abundance of small to medium-sized, nodding flowers in shades of purple, blue, pink, red, and white from midsummer into autumn. Native to southern Europe and western Asia, it is valued for its resistance to clematis wilt — the devastating fungal disease that plagues large-flowered hybrids. Growing 3–4 meters, it can be hard-pruned to the ground each spring (Group 3 pruning), making it the easiest clematis to maintain. Popular cultivars include 'Étoile Violette' and 'Polish Spirit.'
history_text_short: Clematis viticella is native to southern and southeastern Europe including Italy, the Balkans, and Turkey. It was introduced to British horticulture around 1569 by John Gerard, the herbalist, from Italy — one of the earliest exotic clematis species grown in England.
history_text_long:
Clematis viticella is native to southern and southeastern Europe including Italy, the Balkans, and Turkey. It was introduced to British horticulture around 1569 by John Gerard, the herbalist, from Italy — one of the earliest exotic clematis species grown in England, predating the Victorian hybridization boom by nearly three centuries. Its ability to flower prolifically in late summer on new growth means it tolerates aggressive pruning, and it rarely succumbs to Phoma clematidina ("clematis wilt"), the disease that devastates large-flowered C. lanuginosa hybrids.

Modern breeding by Raymond Evison, Brother Stefan Franczak (a Polish Jesuit who bred prolifically in the 1960s-90s), and Wim Snoeijer has produced a range of disease-resistant cultivars including "Étoile Violette," "Polish Spirit," and the Boulevard series. C. viticella parentage is now considered essential to any reliable garden clematis. Clematis viticella has been cultivated in European gardens since the 1500s — it was one of the first clematis species to reach England, documented in 1569.

Italian Renaissance gardens featured it on pergolas and walls. When clematis wilt devastated large-flowered hybrids in the 20th century, viticella cultivars became the saviors of clematis gardening — their natural wilt resistance made them reliable alternatives. The famous partnership of clematis climbing through roses was popularized by Christopher Lloyd at Great Dixter garden in England, and viticella types are ideal for this because their hard annual pruning doesn't damage the host rose.
name_origin: Clematis from Greek 'klema.' Viticella means 'small vine,' a diminutive of Latin 'vitis' (vine).

symbolism_story: Italian Clematis is artistry climbing. Its nodding violet bells thread through trellises and old roses with the deliberate rhythm of a Renaissance vine motif. Beloved in European gardens for centuries, it turns vertical space into composition, rewriting a wall or pergola one elegant flower at a time.

description: Spider Flower is a tall South American annual famous for its unique spidery flowers with extremely long stamens and seedpods radiating outward on airy stems. Growing 3 to 5 feet tall with palmately-compound leaves and a distinctive strong skunk-like scent, it produces large rounded clusters of pink, white, rose, or purple flowers from summer through frost. A back-of-border classic in American cottage and formal gardens.
history_text_short: Spider flower is a tall South American annual famous for its long-stamened airy flower clusters that bloom at the top of stems while seedpods elongate below. Swiss botanist Emile Hassler, who collected extensively in Paraguay, lent his name to the species.
history_text_long:
Cleome hassleriana, the spider flower, is a tall herbaceous annual native to southeastern Brazil, Paraguay, Uruguay, and northern Argentina. Swiss botanist Robert Chodat described it in 1898 and named it for his countryman Emile Hassler, who collected the type specimen during his extensive Paraguayan explorations. The plant produces tall one-meter stems topped by airy racemes of four-petaled pink, white, or purple flowers with protruding spidery stamens, while needle-thin seedpods elongate below the still-blooming inflorescence.

Victorian gardeners popularized it for the back of borders, and the Queen series developed in the mid-20th century standardized cultivars. More recently Proven Winners released the thornless sterile Senorita Rosalita, eliminating prickles and self-seeding, making spider flower easier to integrate into modern landscapes.

Introduced to American Victorian gardens in the 1830s from Paraguay and southern Brazil, spider flower became a staple of cottage and estate gardens. Self-sows freely enough to become a beloved perennial volunteer.
name_origin: 'Cleome' possibly Greek origin, uncertain; 'hassleriana' honors Swiss botanist Emile Hassler (1861-1937) who collected in Paraguay.

By night it shifts roles, its pale petals catching moonlight and feeding hawkmoths and even bats during Night forage. Few flowers manage such grace by day and such usefulness by dark.

description: Rocky Mountain Bee Plant is a native annual wildflower of the North American plains and Rocky Mountain foothills, from Saskatchewan south through Texas and New Mexico. Growing 2 to 4 feet tall with three-part leaves, it produces pink to rose-purple spider-like flower clusters from late spring through fall. Culturally important to Pueblo peoples who harvest leaves for guaco, a traditional pottery paint pigment, and use flowers as a bee forage crop.
history_text_short: Rocky Mountain beeplant is a tall native of western North America that Indigenous peoples used as potherb and as a boiled-down black paint pigment for pueblo pottery. It remains an important restoration and pollinator plant across the Great Plains and Southwest.
history_text_long:
Cleome serrulata, the Rocky Mountain beeplant or stinking clover, is an erect annual native to the western and central United States and Canada, from Minnesota and Saskatchewan through the Great Plains and Rockies to Arizona and New Mexico. American botanist Frederick Traugott Pursh described it in 1813. Indigenous peoples including the Navajo, Hopi, Pueblo, and Lakota used young shoots as a cooked potherb, seeds ground for flour, and boiled-down plant juice as a black paint slip for pottery; the iconic black-on-white designs of Acoma, Zuni, and San Ildefonso pottery trace back in part to this pigment source.

The plant produces bright pink to purple spider-like flowers on tall stems from summer through frost and is a superior nectar source for native bees, from which the common name derives. A signature plant of North American Great Plains and Southwest grasslands.

Hopi, Zuni, and other Puebloan peoples have harvested leaves for over a thousand years to make guaco, a boiled-down black paint used to decorate pottery. Lewis and Clark documented it in 1804 as 'bee plant' for its extraordinary pollinator attraction.
name_origin: The name Rocky Mountain Beeplant points to the Rocky Mountains. 'serrulata' from Latin 'serrula' meaning small saw, for the finely toothed leaf margins.

symbolism_story: Rocky Mountain Beeplant is an ancestral bond between flower and people, its leaves cooked into the black paint that adorns thousand-year-old Puebloan pottery. Across high-desert summers it doubles as a champion native pollinator, feeding bees through brutal drought. In its lavender clouds, ancient art and prairie ecology share the same purple stem.

description: Mountain Sweet Pepperbush or Cinnamonbark Clethra is a southern Appalachian native deciduous shrub growing 8 to 15 feet tall, taller than common summersweet, with fragrant white bottlebrush flowers in midsummer and striking exfoliating cinnamon-brown bark. Prized by collectors for its unique multi-season interest with attractive bark and later flowering in American mountain-style native gardens.
history_text_short: Mountain pepperbush is a southern Appalachian endemic, described by Michaux in 1803. Taller than summersweet and distinguished by exfoliating cinnamon bark, it was collected in the Great Smokies by early American botanists and is valued as a specimen woodland shrub.
history_text_long:
Clethra acuminata grows in cool mountain coves and rocky stream banks of the southern Appalachians, from West Virginia to northern Georgia. The French botanist André Michaux described it in his Flora Boreali-Americana (1803) from specimens collected during his 1787-1796 North American expeditions, including visits to the Carolina and Tennessee mountains. Unlike its shrubby lowland cousin C. alnifolia, it reaches small-tree size (3 to 6 m) with striking exfoliating cinnamon-brown bark reminiscent of Stewartia or Heptacodium.

Its fragrant white flower spikes appear in mid to late summer. It entered British gardens in 1806 via William Curtis but never achieved the horticultural popularity of C. alnifolia. Modern specimen use at the US National Arboretum and Hillier Gardens has renewed interest in it for connoisseur woodland plantings. Native to the Appalachian Mountains from Virginia to Georgia in moist cove forests.
name_origin: The name Mountain Sweet Pepperbush describes its sweet scent or flavor. 'acuminata' from Latin means pointed or tapered, for the leaf tips.

uses_list.text: Summersweet flower spikes carry honey-spice perfume

symbolism_list.description: scent of Appalachian summer forests

symbolism_story: Mountain Sweet Pepperbush perfumes Appalachian summer forests with the meaning of mountain fragrance, a scent that hangs over creek hollows on warm July evenings. In winter, attention shifts to its distinctive cinnamon bark, peeling in pale brown sheets along the trunk and giving the shrub a second season of beauty. To plant Clethra acuminata in the garden is to import a small piece of the southern mountains, both the summer scent and the cold-weather glow of bark.

fragrance.notes: Flowers intensely sweet and spicy, a signature late-summer garden scent.

bloom_tip: Fragrant white or pink bottlebrush spikes July to August

description: Summersweet or Sweet Pepperbush is an eastern North American native deciduous shrub growing 4 to 8 feet tall, producing intensely fragrant white or pink bottlebrush flower spikes in mid to late summer when few other shrubs bloom. The richly-scented flowers draw bees, butterflies, and hummingbirds, and the leaves turn clear yellow in fall. A signature shrub of American coastal and rain gardens.
history_text_short: Summersweet is an eastern North American wetland native described by Linnaeus in 1753. Colonial settlers brewed the bark for skin wounds. Its intensely fragrant late-summer white flower spikes and tolerance of wet soils make it a top pollinator shrub.
history_text_long:
Clethra alnifolia inhabits swamps, wet woods, and coastal pine barrens from Maine to Florida and west to east Texas. Linnaeus described it in Species Plantarum (1753); the epithet alnifolia refers to alder-like leaves. Colonial herbalists used bark decoctions for sores and skin complaints.

John Bartram sent specimens to England in the 1740s, and the species was cultivated in British gardens from the 1750s, valued for filling a gap in the late-summer garden with heavy, sweetly fragrant white flower spikes. Its popularity surged again in the late 20th century with the introductions of the pink 'Ruby Spice' (1992), compact 'Hummingbird' (1990), and 'Sixteen Candles' (2006) by nurseries like Sunny Border and Proven Winners.

It is a major nectar source for bees and butterflies. Native to the eastern United States from Maine to Florida and west to Texas, found in wet coastal areas and stream sides. A 1770s garden import from American colonies to English gardens, now a staple of American native landscape design.
name_origin: The name Sweet Pepperbush describes its sweet scent or flavor. 'Clethra' from Greek 'klethra' meaning alder, for similar leaves; 'alnifolia' from Latin means alder-leaved.

As a piece of coastal heritage it has lined Atlantic wetlands from Maine to Florida for millennia. To inhale it is to know exactly where, and when, you are.

description: Japanese Clethra is an elegant deciduous shrub or small tree reaching 10-20 feet, distinguished by beautifully mottled exfoliating bark in shades of gray, cinnamon, and cream. Fragrant white flowers appear in drooping panicles from late summer into fall, attracting late-season pollinators. Autumn foliage turns brilliant yellow to orange-red. A superb four-season shrub for woodland gardens, it thrives in acidic soils with ample moisture.
history_text_short: Japanese clethra is native to Japan, Korea, and eastern China. Siebold and Zuccarini described it in 1839. Tall narrow racemes of fragrant white flowers in midsummer and spectacular exfoliating cinnamon bark on mature stems make it one of the finest small flowering trees for the woodland garden.
history_text_long:
Clethra barbinervis is native to Japan, Korea, and eastern China. Siebold and Zuccarini described it in 1839, and the epithet barbinervis means bearded-veined, referring to hairs along the leaf veins. Unlike the shrubby North American summersweet, Japanese clethra becomes a small, open tree with graceful midsummer racemes of fragrant white bell flowers.

Its second act is the bark: mature trunks exfoliate into smooth patches of gray-green, cinnamon, and ochre, giving winter gardens the polished beauty usually associated with stewartias. Introduced to Europe in the late 19th century, it has remained more a collector's tree than a mass-market shrub, but mature specimens are often the quiet masterpieces of woodland gardens. It offers fragrance, fall color, and bark in one plant, which is rare enough to make plant lovers remember it.
name_origin: The name Japanese Clethra points to Japan. From Greek 'klethra' (alder, referring to similar leaves); 'barbinervis' means bearded veins.

Its fragrant summer racemes give way to autumn color, then to a winter trunk whose mottled bark rewards anyone who steps close. This is a plant for the patient observer — a small tree of enduring loveliness that proves the deepest pleasures often live in the details rather than the dramatic gesture.

description: Japanese Cleyera, or Sakaki, is a refined evergreen shrub or small tree to 10-15 feet with glossy leathery dark green leaves that emerge coppery-red. Small fragrant creamy-white flowers in early summer are followed by dark red berries ripening black. Sacred in Shinto tradition and widely used in temple plantings, it is prized in Southern US gardens as a durable evergreen for shade or sun with a graceful upright habit.
history_text_short: Japanese cleyera, or sakaki, is native to Japan, Taiwan, Korea, and southern China. Thunberg described it in 1783. In Shinto ritual, glossy evergreen branches are offered at shrines and home altars, making this modest tree one of Japan's most sacred plants.
history_text_long:
Cleyera japonica grows in Japan, Taiwan, southern Korea, and southern China. Thunberg described it in 1783 from material gathered during his Japanese residency. In Japan the tree is called sakaki, a name bound to Shinto ritual for more than a thousand years.

Evergreen branches are offered as tamagushi at shrines and funerals, placed on household altar shelves, and renewed regularly as a living connection between the domestic and the sacred. The tree itself is planted around shrine precincts and boundaries, where its glossy leaves and modest cream flowers matter less as ornament than as presence. It was introduced to Western cultivation in the 19th century but remains uncommon outside mild coastal gardens and specialist collections. Variegated selections such as 'Fortunei' and 'Tricolor' bring its sacred evergreen form into ornamental use.
name_origin: The name Bird Claw Cleyera, Japanese Cleyera points to Japan. Genus honors Andreas Cleyer, 17th-century Dutch physician in Japan; 'japonica' means of Japan.

symbolism_story: Sakaki, the Japanese Cleyera, is sacred to Shinto tradition, its branches carried at shrines as instruments of sanctity. Paired with purity, its glossy leaves are used to cleanse and bless ritual spaces, an emblem of the holy and the unseen. To plant it is to keep a quietly reverent presence in the garden — a tree that has, for centuries, held space for prayer.

description: Codiaeum variegatum is the correct botanical name for the plant commonly sold as 'Croton.' This species and Croton variegatum refer to the same plant — a vividly colored tropical shrub from the Euphorbia family. See Croton variegatum for full details. The genus Codiaeum contains about 17 species, all from the Malay Archipelago and Pacific Islands, but C. variegatum is the only one widely cultivated. The name confusion between Codiaeum and Croton persists in the nursery trade, though they are botanically distinct genera.
history_text_short: The Garden Croton is native to Malaysia, Indonesia, and the western Pacific. It has been cultivated in Pacific island cultures for centuries as a hedge and ceremonial plant; hundreds of vivid cultivars now exist.
history_text_long:
Codiaeum variegatum is native to Malaysia, Indonesia, the Pacific islands from New Guinea to Fiji, and northern Australia, where it grows as an evergreen shrub to six meters tall in coastal and lowland forest. Pacific island peoples have cultivated it for centuries: in Polynesian, Melanesian, and New Guinea cultures it is planted as hedging to mark land boundaries, used in ceremony and funerary practice, and paired with specific color variants carrying ritual meaning. Western horticulture adopted it in the 19th century, and intensive breeding — especially in Florida and the Netherlands — has produced several hundred named cultivars showing yellow, orange, red, purple, and near-black variegation in a remarkable range of leaf shapes.

Its milky latex contains irritant diterpene esters. The naming confusion between Codiaeum and Croton dates to 1753, when Linnaeus grouped many unrelated tropical plants under 'Croton.' Later botanists separated them, but the nursery trade never caught up.

True Croton is a massive genus of over 1,200 species in the spurge family, mostly non-ornamental. Codiaeum has only 17 species, with C. variegatum being the sole garden star. The plant played a role in colonial botanical gardens across the British Empire — Kew Gardens distributed thousands of cultivars to gardens in India, Singapore, and Australia during the 19th century.
name_origin: Codiaeum from Malay 'kodiho.' Variegatum means 'variegated.' Often mislabeled as Croton, which is a separate genus in the same family.

symbolism_list.description: Refuses to blend in — its riot of color represents fearless self-expression

symbolism_story: The Variegated Croton refuses to blend in, its riot of red, yellow, orange, and green leaves embodying boldness and fearless self-expression. It is often read as a flower of tropical confidence, asking no permission to be brilliant in a room of muted greens. To live with it is to accept that quiet good taste is not the only kind of beauty, and that some plants exist precisely to challenge the palette.

description: Autumn Crocus or Meadow Saffron is a European corm hardy in USDA zones 4-8, producing leafless pink-lavender crocus-like flowers that emerge from bare ground in September and October. The broad strap-like leaves follow in spring and die back by early summer. Often confused with true crocus but unrelated, it is a treasured fall bulb for American gardens, adding unexpected color when most other perennials are winding down.
history_text_short: Autumn crocus, native to Europe, was described by Linnaeus in 1753. Though resembling a crocus, it is in the lily family. Its alkaloid colchicine, used since ancient Egypt for gout, remains a modern pharmaceutical and a key tool in plant chromosome research.
history_text_long:
Colchicum autumnale grows in damp meadows across Europe from the British Isles to the Balkans. Linnaeus described it in Species Plantarum (1753). The genus name comes from Colchis, the ancient kingdom on the eastern Black Sea associated with the sorceress Medea in Greek myth.

The Ebers Papyrus of ancient Egypt (c.1500 BCE) records its use for rheumatic pain and swollen joints, a treatment continued in Greek, Arab, and medieval European medicine. In 1820 French chemists Pelletier and Caventou isolated the alkaloid colchicine from the corms; it is still the first-line drug for acute gout and familial Mediterranean fever. Colchicine also blocks mitosis, and was used from 1937 onward by plant breeders to double chromosome numbers — a technique that produced seedless grapes and polyploid ornamentals.

Highly toxic if eaten. Native to Europe and North Africa, cultivated since medieval times as a medicinal plant for gout. Colchicine extracted from the corms remains a modern gout medication. Introduced to American gardens in the 1700s, it has long been a heirloom fall-blooming bulb especially in older Southern gardens.
name_origin: 'Colchicum' from Colchis, the ancient Black Sea kingdom where Medea allegedly used it in myths; 'autumnale' refers to the autumn flowering.

symbolism_story: Autumn Crocus brings beauty at the wrong time, and that is its magic. Leafless lavender cups rise from bare soil when the garden should be closing down, a last impossible gesture before winter. Its deeper symbolism is paradox: elegance from a plant whose chemistry demands respect.

description: Coleus is a tropical Southeast Asian tender perennial grown as an annual across the US, beloved not for flowers but for spectacular multicolored foliage in near-infinite combinations of lime, burgundy, red, pink, yellow, orange, and near-black. Growing 10 to 36 inches tall depending on cultivar, modern sun-tolerant varieties have transformed American shade and sun container gardening since the 2000s.
history_text_short: Coleus, or painted nettle, is a Southeast Asian tropical perennial prized for kaleidoscopic foliage rather than flowers. Victorian Britain saw a coleus mania, and Ball Horticultural's 21st-century sun-tolerant introductions brought a second global renaissance.
history_text_long:
Coleus scutellarioides, long cultivated as Solenostemon scutellarioides or Plectranthus scutellarioides, is a tender perennial in the mint family native to Southeast Asia from India through Indonesia and into northern Australia. Dutch gardeners introduced the plant to Europe from Java in 1851, triggering Britain's Coleus Mania of the 1860s and 1870s, during which nurseries marketed hundreds of named leaf forms. The plant's riotous combinations of green, yellow, pink, red, orange, and purple on leaves of every shape returned to horticultural favor with Ball FloraPlant's ColorBlaze series, Proven Winners' Under the Sea selections, and the Main Street, FlameThrower, and Great Falls programs.

Modern breeding also delivered sun-tolerance, restraining the old shade-only reputation and expanding coleus into full-sun bedding across North America. Cultivated in Southeast Asia for centuries, introduced to Victorian American gardens as a greenhouse bedding plant in the 1860s.

The Victorian 'coleus craze' produced thousands of cultivars. Modern sun-tolerant hybrids like 'ColorBlaze' and 'Sun Coleus' revolutionized American container gardening in the 2000s.
name_origin: 'scutellarioides' means resembling Scutellaria (skullcap); long known as Coleus, briefly moved to Plectranthus and Solenostemon, now back to Coleus.

Modern gardeners keep it for the same reason, though with looser rules: the plant turns shade and containers into a gallery of foliage rather than a wait for flowers.

description: Colocasia esculenta, commonly known as taro, is one of humanity's oldest cultivated crops. Its massive heart-shaped leaves on tall petioles create a bold tropical statement, and the starchy underground corm is a staple food for hundreds of millions of people across Asia, Africa, and the Pacific Islands. In gardens, ornamental varieties like 'Black Magic' with dark purple leaves are grown for dramatic foliage. It thrives in moist to wet conditions — naturally a wetland plant — and can be grown at pond margins or in consistently moist garden soil.
history_text_short: Taro is one of humanity's oldest cultivated food plants, domesticated in tropical Asia over 9,000 years ago. The starchy corm feeds hundreds of millions globally; raw leaves and corms are toxic due to calcium oxalate.
history_text_long:
Colocasia esculenta — taro — is among the very earliest cultivated food plants in human history, with archaeological evidence of cultivation in New Guinea and Southeast Asia stretching back more than nine thousand years. It spread with Austronesian voyagers across the Pacific, where it remains a staple in Hawaii (kalo, the base of poi), Samoa, and Fiji; it became fundamental in parts of West Africa, the Caribbean (where it is known as dasheen, eddo, or malanga), and southern India and Japan (as satoimo). The corm must be cooked long enough to destroy its calcium oxalate raphides, which otherwise cause severe oral irritation.

Ornamental forms with black leaves ('Black Magic') and elephant-ear cultivars are popular summer garden plants in temperate regions. Taro is one of the oldest cultivated plants on Earth, domesticated in Southeast Asia at least 10,000 years ago — predating rice cultivation. Polynesian voyagers carried it across the Pacific in their canoes, making it foundational to Hawaiian, Samoan, and Maori diets.

In Hawaiian creation mythology, taro is the elder brother of humanity — the first-born child of the sky father Wakea, named Haloa, whose buried body sprouted into the first taro plant. This sacred relationship means taro is not merely food but family. Today, taro feeds over 400 million people worldwide.
name_origin: Colocasia from Greek 'kolokasia,' an ancient name for the edible root. Esculenta means 'edible' in Latin.

symbolism_list.description: One of humanity's oldest crops, it symbolizes sustenance and ancestral care

symbolism_story: Taro is nourishment carried across millennia and oceans — one of humanity's oldest cultivated crops, fed to children in Hawaiian, West African, and Southeast Asian kitchens for thousands of years. Its enormous heart-shaped leaves and starchy corms speak of ancestral care, the hands that pounded poi and pounded fufu so the next generation would eat. It is the plant that quietly raised civilizations.

fragrance.notes: Large spathe flowers have a strong fruity-fermented scent in full bloom.

bloom_tip: Produces a large fragrant spadix; grown primarily for its enormous foliage

description: Giant Elephant Ear is a colossal tropical aroid native to mainland Southeast Asia, known for producing some of the largest leaves of any cultivated plant. A single leaf blade can measure 4 to 5 feet long and 3 to 4 feet wide, held aloft on thick, sturdy petioles that can reach 6 feet, giving the plant an overall height of 6 to 9 feet. The leaves are a distinctive blue-green with prominent pale veins and a waxy, water-repellent surface — raindrops bead and roll like mercury across the blade. Unlike its cousin Colocasia esculenta (taro), the giant elephant ear is grown primarily as an ornamental rather than a food crop. It thrives in rich, boggy soil or even standing water, making it excellent for pond margins and rain gardens. The plant spreads via offsets but is less aggressive than common taro. In temperate regions, the large corm must be lifted before frost and stored dry over winter. The cultivar 'Thailand Giant' is especially popular for its record-breaking leaf size.
history_text_short: Giant elephant ear is native to Southeast Asia, from Bangladesh and southern China through Indochina to Java. Its arrow-shaped leaves up to 1.5 m long make it one of the most dramatic foliage plants of subtropical gardens. Petioles are eaten as a vegetable in Vietnamese and Thai cuisine ("bạc hà").
history_text_long:
Colocasia gigantea is native to Southeast Asia — Bangladesh, southern China, Myanmar, Thailand, Vietnam, Laos, Cambodia, Malaysia, and Indonesia (Java) — where it grows as an understory plant in moist tropical forests and stream margins. Mature plants produce immense arrow-shaped leaves 1-1.5 meters long on petioles 1.5-2 meters tall, making it among the largest-leaved herbaceous plants grown in temperate gardens as a subtropical foliage accent. It is closely related to taro (C. esculenta), but whereas taro is cultivated primarily for its edible corms, C. gigantea is more often cultivated for its edible petioles: in Vietnamese cuisine the long succulent petioles are called "bạc hà" and are a traditional ingredient of canh chua (sour fish soup), where their spongy aerated tissue absorbs the broth; in Thai cuisine the petioles are used in various curries and soups. The plant's corms, unlike true taro, are generally not eaten.

All parts contain calcium oxalate raphides — needle-shaped crystals — which make raw material painfully irritating to mucous membranes; proper cooking (and careful preparation) dissolves/neutralizes the oxalate. Popular ornamental selections include "Thailand Giant" (very large leaves) and "Laosy Giant." Colocasia gigantea has been grown in Southeast Asian gardens for centuries, though it lacks the deep agricultural history of its edible cousin, taro.

The species gained worldwide horticultural fame in the early 2000s when the cultivar 'Thailand Giant' set records for enormous leaf size. In its native habitat, the plants grow along streams and in seasonally flooded forests. The genus Colocasia contains about 20 species, all native to tropical Asia.
name_origin: 'Colocasia' derives from the Greek 'kolokasia,' an ancient name for the edible root of a related plant. 'Gigantea' is Latin for giant, an apt description of this species' enormous leaves.

symbolism_list.description: the massive leaves represent magnificence and awe-inspiring scale
the umbrella-like leaves symbolize shelter and guardianship

symbolism_story: Giant Elephant Ear is Grandeur in leaf form — single fronds large enough to dwarf an adult, each one an unfolding green flag. Its broad form also offers Protection, casting deep shade like a living umbrella over the plants and creatures beneath. To stand under one is to feel the tropics translated into pure scale.

bloom_tip: Sow in fall for spring bloom in mild climates; thin seedlings to 15-20 cm spacing for strong stems

description: Consolida ajacis, the larkspur or rocket larkspur, is an elegant annual native to the Mediterranean region, closely related to delphiniums but easier to grow from seed. It produces tall spires of spurred flowers in vivid shades of blue, purple, pink, and white that reach 60 to 120 cm tall, adding vertical drama to summer gardens. The deeply divided, fern-like foliage provides a fine-textured backdrop to the flower spikes. Larkspur is one of the finest cut flowers for fresh arrangements, and its blooms also dry exceptionally well, retaining color for months. The plant prefers cool growing conditions and is best sown directly in fall or very early spring in mild climates, as it dislikes heat and humidity. It makes an excellent successor to spring bulbs, filling the garden with color from late spring through midsummer. Larkspur self-sows reliably in congenial climates, creating casual drifts of color year after year. All parts of the plant are toxic, containing diterpene alkaloids similar to those in Aconitum (monkshood).
history_text_short: Rocket larkspur is native to the Mediterranean basin. The annual relative of perennial Delphinium, it is widely grown for its spire-like flower stalks in blue, purple, pink, and white. All parts are toxic — larkspur alkaloids cause significant livestock poisoning in the western US, particularly in young cattle on spring rangeland.
history_text_long:
Consolida ajacis (in some classifications Delphinium ajacis) is native to the Mediterranean basin and southwest Asia. It is an annual close relative of the perennial larkspurs (Delphinium) and was formerly placed in that genus before being moved to Consolida based on morphological differences; some taxonomic authorities still treat it as Delphinium. It produces upright branched 60-90 cm flower spikes densely covered with spurred two-lipped flowers typically in blue, violet, pink, and white, blooming from late spring through early summer. The species is one of the classic cottage garden, cutting garden, and cutting-flower industry annuals, grown from seed either autumn-sown (for larger plants and earlier flowering) or spring-sown in colder climates.

Like all members of the larkspur/delphinium tribe, it contains highly toxic diterpenoid alkaloids (methyllycaconitine, lycoctonine, and related compounds) in all parts, which affect the neuromuscular junction and can cause rapid death in grazing livestock — particularly cattle, which are unusually susceptible. Tall larkspur poisoning is one of the largest cattle-loss causes on mountain spring range in the western United States. The name "ajacis" refers to the Greek hero Ajax — in the myth, when Ajax killed himself over grief about the Trojan War, his blood turned to the larkspur flower, whose markings supposedly spell AIA (the first letters of his name in Greek).

The name 'larkspur' comes from the flower's long, backward-pointing spur, which was thought to resemble the claw of a lark. In Greek mythology, the flower was said to have sprung from the blood of Ajax after his death in the Trojan War — the markings on the petals were read as the letters 'AI,' the Greek cry of mourning, giving the species name 'ajacis.' For centuries, European herbalists used larkspur tinctures externally to treat head lice and scabies, though internal use was recognized as dangerous. The Victorians adored it as a garden and cut flower, and it became a symbol of an open heart and ardent attachment in the language of flowers. Today it remains indispensable in the cut flower industry.
name_origin: Consolida comes from Latin 'consolidare' (to make whole), reflecting old wound lore. Ajacis honors the Greek hero Ajax from the Trojan War.

uses_list.text: Tall spurred spires star in cottage and cutting gardens
Vivid blue, purple, pink spikes evoke easy-grown delphiniums
Stems dry well for everlasting wreaths and arrangements

symbolism_list.description: The airy, spurred flowers evoke a carefree spirit and levity
Victorian symbol of ardent attachment and willingness to love freely

symbolism_story: Doubtful Knight's-Spur is lightness on a stem, its airy spurred florets rising like little notes on a staff of green. In Victorian floriography it was the open heart, an emblem of ardent attachment freely given. To grow larkspur in the cottage border is to plant a flower that confesses easily and laughs while doing it.

description: Forking Larkspur is a European annual related to delphinium, producing slender 18 to 36 inch spikes of violet-blue, purple, pink, or white spurred flowers in early summer. Self-sows reliably, making it a classic cottage-garden annual that returns year after year. Taller and earlier blooming than Consolida ajacis.
history_text_short: Forking larkspur is a European annual in the buttercup family whose spurred blue-violet flowers colored medieval fields of rye and wheat. Now rare in many European countries because of herbicide-intensive farming, it remains a classic cottage and meadow annual.
history_text_long:
Consolida regalis, commonly called forking larkspur or royal knight's-spur, is an annual herb native to Europe, North Africa, and western Asia. Swedish botanist Samuel Gray described the current name in 1821, reclassifying the species from the earlier Delphinium consolida of Linnaeus. For centuries the plant was a common cornfield weed across Europe, its spurred deep blue to violet flowers mingling with corn poppies, cornflowers, and corn marigolds.

Intensive herbicide use since the mid-20th century has made Consolida regalis rare in many European countries, spurring agri-environment seed mixes aimed at restoring cornfield flora. Garden cultivars have been selected for larger flowers and wider color range, though all Consolida species are poisonous to livestock and humans due to diterpenoid alkaloids.

Native to European and Western Asian grainfields where it was historically a common grain-field weed, introduced to American gardens by colonists in the 1700s.
name_origin: 'Consolida' comes from Latin 'consolidare' meaning to make whole, an old herbal reference; 'regalis' means royal, for the spike flower form.

uses_list.text: Slender blue larkspur spikes cut fresh or dried

symbolism_story: Forking Larkspur's flower meaning is swiftness, for the plant is quick to bloom from seed and quick to self-sow itself across a meadow garden. Its longer story is cottage heritage, the classic European grain-field flower that once threaded blue through wheat and rye before modern herbicides cleared the cornfields. In the language of old fields, consolida suggests a vanished agricultural world where weeds and crops once grew together in something like accidental beauty.

fragrance.notes: Iconic sweet-green floral scent; reproduced in perfumery as hydroxycitronellal and related muguet accords.

description: Convallaria majalis, lily of the valley, produces arching stems of tiny, pure white, bell-shaped flowers with one of the sweetest, most recognizable fragrances in the plant kingdom. Despite its delicate appearance, it is an aggressive spreader that forms dense ground cover via underground rhizomes. Native to Europe and temperate Asia, it blooms in late spring in shade. All parts are highly toxic — the cardiac glycosides are similar to foxglove. It was a staple of royal weddings, appearing in Kate Middleton's 2011 bridal bouquet. Red berries follow the flowers in autumn.
history_text_short: Lily-of-the-valley is a Eurasian woodland perennial woven into European folk tradition — Norse myth, the French "Muguet du 1er mai," and royal weddings including Kate Middleton's. All parts are highly toxic, and its fragrance is one of the most imitated in perfumery.
history_text_long:
Convallaria majalis is native to temperate woodlands across Europe and eastern North America. Medieval Christian tradition tied it to the Virgin Mary's tears at the Crucifixion; Norse myth made it sacred to Ostara. The French custom of giving lily-of-the-valley on May 1 ("Muguet du 1er mai") dates to a gift from King Charles IX in 1561 and became legally enshrined as a duty-free street-vending day. Christian Dior made the flower his personal talisman and the basis of the 1956 perfume Diorissimo by Edmond Roudnitska — one of the most admired lily-of-the-valley compositions in perfumery, notable because the flower yields no usable essential oil and must be synthesized.

All parts contain cardiac glycosides (convallatoxin) and are dangerously toxic. The plant featured in royal wedding bouquets including Queen Elizabeth II (1947) and Kate Middleton (2011). Lily of the valley is the national flower of Finland and the traditional flower of May Day in France, where 'muguet' sprigs are exchanged as tokens of good luck on May 1st — over 60 million stems are sold on that single day.

Christian legend says the flowers sprang from Eve's tears when she was expelled from Eden, or from the Virgin Mary's tears at the cross. The fragrance is so complex that it could not be synthetically replicated until 1956, when Firmenich created 'Muguet des Bois.' Despite extreme toxicity — the same cardiac glycosides as foxglove — it appeared in Kate Middleton's royal wedding bouquet in 2011.
name_origin: Convallaria from Latin 'convallis' (valley). Majalis means 'of May,' for its May blooming time.

uses_list.text: White nodding bells distilled for classic perfumery essence

symbolism_list.description: A May Day symbol across Europe, representing spring's return and renewed joy

symbolism_story: Lily of the valley is often read as a flower of returning happiness, its first green spears unfurling at exactly the moment European winter relinquishes its grip. On May Day across France, sprigs are exchanged hand to hand as a small portable promise that joy, like the season, comes back. Few flowers are so saturated in collective memory of relief, or carry so much fragrance in such modest white bells.

description: Field Bindweed is a Eurasian perennial vine with creeping and climbing stems, arrow-shaped leaves, and small white-pink trumpet flowers, one of the most destructive agricultural weeds worldwide. Deep taproots reach 20 feet and lateral roots spread 10 feet per year, making it virtually impossible to eradicate. Listed as noxious in nearly every US state and a catastrophic weed of American gardens, row crops, and perennial plantings.
history_text_short: Convolvulus arvensis, field bindweed, is a deep-rooted perennial native to Europe and western Asia whose twining stems and pink-striped white funnel flowers are beautiful but extremely invasive. Its taproot can reach six metres deep, regenerating from tiny fragments, and it is rated among the worst agricultural weeds worldwide.
history_text_long:
Convolvulus arvensis, field bindweed, is a wiry perennial vine in the morning glory family native to Europe, North Africa, and western Asia. Ancient Greek and Roman writers noted its tenacity, and European settlers carried it worldwide in contaminated grain, where it is now one of the most serious agricultural weeds on every inhabited continent. The species combines prodigious seed longevity (up to fifty years in soil) with a taproot that penetrates six meters or more, branching laterally just below cultivation depth to send up new shoots from every fragment left by tillage.

Its delicate pink-and-white funnel flowers open in morning sun and close by afternoon, and the plant contains mildly toxic tropane and resinous glycosides that cause digestive upset in livestock. Biological control with gall mites has had partial success.

Native to Europe and Asia, Field Bindweed arrived in North America in the 1700s and is now one of the most widespread and destructive weeds in the US, listed noxious in nearly every state. Seeds remain viable in soil for 60 years, and deep perennial roots survive tilling, herbicide, and drought, making eradication virtually impossible once established.
name_origin: 'Convolvulus' from Latin 'convolvere' meaning to entwine, for the climbing habit; 'arvensis' means of fields.

uses_list.text: Flowers feed small bees, though the vine is often a serious weed

symbolism_list.description: smothers crops and gardens

symbolism_story: Field Bindweed is the patron of suffocating persistence, twining over crops and gardens with relentless grace. Its trumpets are pretty, but its true power lies underground in roots that descend twenty feet and sprawl ten feet outward each year. For farmers and gardeners across temperate continents, bindweed has become a humbling lesson in how a single rooted intruder can refuse, with quiet stubbornness, ever to be conquered.

description: Large-flowered Tickseed is a short-lived native perennial of the south-central US, 12–24 inches tall, with broad golden-yellow daisy flowers 2–3 inches across from early summer to fall. Widely planted as a bright mass-flowering perennial in American gardens and roadside wildflower seedings. Cultivars 'Early Sunrise' and 'Sunburst' offer double forms; newer hybrids extend color to pink, red, and bicolor.
history_text_short: Large-flowered tickseed is native to the southeastern US and adjacent Mexico. Described by botanist Stephen Elliott in 1821, it became a foundational garden coreopsis and parent of many modern hybrids since the 1990s.
history_text_long:
Coreopsis grandiflora occurs naturally from Kansas through Missouri, Arkansas, and Texas east to Georgia. Stephen Elliott described it in his Sketch of the Botany of South Carolina and Georgia (1821). Unlike the threadleaf species, it has broad lance-shaped foliage and bold 2-inch yellow daisies.

European horticulturists introduced cultivars such as 'Sunray' in the 20th century. Starting in the 1990s, breeders at companies like Itsaul Plants and Terra Nova used it as a parent for the Big Bang series and other complex hybrids featuring red, pink, and bicolor flowers. Though a short-lived perennial, its prolific seeding and deadheading response make it a garden mainstay.

Native from Missouri to Florida and west to New Mexico. 'Early Sunrise' won the All-America Selections award in 1989, becoming one of the first perennials ever to win AAS, and widely spread through American roadside and garden seedings. It is the state wildflower of Mississippi.
name_origin: Genus means 'bug-like' for seed shape; 'grandiflora' means 'large-flowered'.

uses_list.text: Yellow daisy flowers draw bees and hoverflies all summer

Cheerful yellow blooms last well in casual bouquets

symbolism_story: Large-Flowered Tickseed is pure cheerfulness — bright gold daisy-like flowers that lift any garden bed they're placed in. Paired with warmth, the blooms read like distilled summer sunshine, easy company for bees and butterflies alike. It is often read as a flower of uncomplicated gladness: nothing rare or precious, just dependable, sun-soaked joy returning year after year.

description: Coreopsis lanceolata, lanceleaf coreopsis or tickseed, is a cheerful North American native wildflower that paints fields and roadsides golden-yellow from late spring through mid summer. Each flower features bright yellow ray petals with notched or lobed tips surrounding a compact golden disc, creating a simple, sunny charm that epitomizes the American wildflower meadow. Growing 30–60 cm tall with narrow, lance-shaped basal leaves, it forms tidy clumps that spread slowly by short rhizomes and self-seeding. It is extraordinarily easy to grow, thriving in poor, dry soil and full sun with almost zero maintenance — in fact, rich soil and too much water make it flop and reduce its lifespan. The flowers attract native bees, small butterflies, and beneficial insects, while goldfinches feast on the seeds in autumn. Deadheading extends bloom for weeks. It is the state wildflower of Mississippi and a foundation species for highway wildflower plantings across the southeastern United States. An ideal starter plant for anyone beginning a native wildflower garden.
history_text_short: Lance-leaved tickseed is native to the central and southeastern United States. The state wildflower of Florida and Mississippi, its bright yellow daisy flowers and easy-care habit have made it one of the most widely used native wildflowers in North American highway seed mixes and meadow plantings.
history_text_long:
Coreopsis lanceolata is native to the central and southeastern United States, from the Great Plains east through the Midwest and Southeast. It produces abundant bright golden-yellow daisy-like flowers 4-6 cm across on wiry 40-60 cm stems from late spring through summer. The species is one of the foundational components of US roadside wildflower seed mixes — it was a major component of the "Lady Bird Johnson" native roadside planting initiative of the 1960s that transformed interstate highway design from manicured turfgrass to native flower meadow, and remains a staple of USDA NRCS (Natural Resources Conservation Service) prairie and pollinator seed specifications.

It is the state wildflower of Mississippi (designated 1991), and a group of Coreopsis species collectively including C. lanceolata is the state wildflower of Florida (designated 1991) — both reflecting the strong cultural and ecological association of the species with southeastern American roadsides and meadows. The species is an excellent nectar source for a wide range of native bees, small butterflies, and syrphid flies.

In landscape horticulture it is a tough, drought-tolerant, short-lived perennial (individual plants often last only 2-3 years) that regenerates reliably from seed. Popular named cultivars include "Sterntaler," "Baby Sun," and the compact "Sunray." Coreopsis lanceolata is native to prairies, open woodlands, and roadsides from the Great Lakes to the Gulf of Mexico.
name_origin: Coreopsis from Greek 'koris' (bedbug) and 'opsis' (appearance), referring to the seed's resemblance to a small insect. Lanceolata means 'lance-shaped,' describing the leaves.

uses_list.text: Golden-yellow daisies fill meadows and roadsides for months
Native nectar source for bees and butterflies
Seeds eaten by goldfinches and other songbirds

symbolism_list.description: Sunny golden flowers that radiate optimism and simple, uncomplicated happiness
Blooms reliably with minimal care, embodying effortless joy and contentment

symbolism_story: Lance-Leaved Coreopsis radiates cheerfulness, its sunny golden flowers an open expression of optimism and uncomplicated happiness. Blooming reliably with minimal care, it earns its old garden name of always happy, a flower that offers joy without demanding effort in return. It is the bloom of effortless contentment, proof that beauty can also be easy, generous, and freely given.

bloom_tip: Pink daisies summer to early fall

description: Pink Tickseed is a rare native perennial of the northeastern US Atlantic coastal plain, 12–18 inches tall, with fine foliage and small pink or rose daisy flowers with yellow centers. Forms spreading mats by rhizomes—more moisture-loving than other Coreopsis. The cultivar 'American Dream' was the original pink coneflower widely sold in American nurseries; newer Color Wheel and Li'l Bang series extend the range. Hardy zones 4–8.
history_text_short: Pink tickseed is a rare wetland coreopsis native to coastal plain ponds from Nova Scotia to Georgia. Described by Thomas Nuttall in 1818, it is globally imperiled in the wild but popularized in gardens by the cultivar 'American Dream' in the 1980s.
history_text_long:
Coreopsis rosea inhabits seasonally inundated coastal plain ponds and wet sandy shores, a specialized habitat that has become increasingly fragmented. Thomas Nuttall described the species in 1818. Unique among coreopsis for its pink ray flowers and threadleaf foliage, it remained a botanical rarity until the cultivar 'American Dream' was introduced around 1983, presenting rich rose-pink flowers on compact plants.

This cultivar and later selections like 'Sweet Dreams' and 'Heaven's Gate' made it a garden staple. It requires moisture unlike most coreopsis, making it valuable for rain gardens. Wild populations are tracked as globally vulnerable (G3) by NatureServe, threatened by hydrological changes and development. Native to wet coastal plain habitats from Nova Scotia to Georgia—a rare and localized species. 'American Dream' was introduced in the 1980s and brought pink coreopsis into mainstream American horticulture.
name_origin: Genus means 'bug-like' for seed shape; 'rosea' means 'rose-pink'.

uses_list.text: Pink daisies attract small native bees and butterflies
Threadleaf clumps spread to fill sunny moist edges
Long-blooming pink tickseed for native perennial borders

symbolism_list.description: soft pink evokes tenderness
Atlantic coastal plain native

symbolism_story: Rose Coreopsis carries gentle affection, its soft pink rays evoking tenderness rather than the brash gold of its sunnier cousins. It is a child of Atlantic coastal plain heritage, native to wet meadows and pond edges along the eastern seaboard. A wildflower for tender hearts and damp ground, where understatement does the slow, steady work of charm.

bloom_tip: Golden daisies early summer to frost

description: Threadleaf Coreopsis is a native perennial of the eastern and southeastern US, 18–30 inches tall, with fine thread-like foliage and masses of small golden-yellow daisy flowers from early summer to frost. Drought-tolerant, deer-resistant, and a pollinator favorite. The cultivar 'Moonbeam' was Perennial Plant of the Year in 1992 and remains one of the most planted perennials in American gardens. 'Zagreb' offers a slightly more compact golden form.
history_text_short: Threadleaf coreopsis is native to the eastern US, described by Linnaeus in 1753. The cultivar 'Moonbeam' revolutionized American perennial gardens when it won Perennial Plant of the Year in 1992 for its soft yellow flowers and heat tolerance.
history_text_long:
Coreopsis verticillata ranges from Maryland to Florida on sandy or rocky soils. Linnaeus named it in 1753 referencing its whorled (verticillate) leaf arrangement. It remained a wild curiosity until the late 20th century when the cultivar 'Moonbeam', a pale primrose-yellow sport, appeared in American nurseries.

The Perennial Plant Association named it Perennial Plant of the Year in 1992, triggering explosive commercial success. 'Zagreb' with deeper gold flowers followed. These cultivars transformed sunny border design throughout North America and Europe, offering long bloom, drought tolerance, and fine-textured foliage.

Molecular studies suggest 'Moonbeam' may be a hybrid rather than pure verticillata, but the name has become horticulturally entrenched. Native to the eastern US. 'Moonbeam', discovered and introduced to commerce in the 1980s, was named Perennial Plant of the Year in 1992 by the Perennial Plant Association, cementing threadleaf coreopsis as a top American perennial.
name_origin: Genus from Greek 'koris' (bug) and 'opsis' (appearance) for the seed shape; 'verticillata' means 'whorled' for the leaf arrangement.

uses_list.text: Yellow daisies feed bees and butterflies all summer
Airy stems prized for casual summer bouquets

symbolism_list.description: never-ending sunny blooms
thrives on neglect

symbolism_story: Whorled Coreopsis is always cheerful, its threadlike leaves and golden daisies bobbing through the heat of summer with apparent indifference to drought. Resilience runs through its roots — this is a plant that thrives on a little neglect and rewards forgetfulness with another flush of bloom. Its meaning is honest, durable optimism: sunshine that does not require constant tending.

fragrance.notes: Leaf with distinctive citrus-soap aroma (the "soap" perception is genetically mediated); seed with warm citrus-spice notes.

bloom_tip: Bolts quickly in heat; sow every 3 weeks for continuous harvest; let some flower for seeds
fruit_tip: Round seeds are the spice coriander; harvest when brown

description: Coriandrum sativum, cilantro/coriander, is a dual-purpose herb — the fresh leaves (cilantro) are essential in Mexican, Thai, Indian, and Chinese cuisines, while the dried seeds (coriander) are a foundational spice. The plant is deeply polarizing: genetic research shows that OR6A2 gene variants make some people perceive cilantro as soapy. Growing 30–60 cm tall, it bolts quickly in heat, producing lacy white or pink flowers that become round coriander seeds. Native to the Mediterranean and Middle East, it has been cultivated for over 5,000 years.
history_text_short: Coriandrum sativum is probably native to the eastern Mediterranean or southwest Asia. Seeds have been recovered from the Nahal Hemar cave in Israel dating to approximately 6000 BCE, making it one of the earliest-cultivated spices.
history_text_long:
Coriandrum sativum is probably native to the eastern Mediterranean or southwest Asia. Seeds have been recovered from the Nahal Hemar cave in Israel dating to approximately 6000 BCE, making it one of the earliest-cultivated spices. Egyptian pharaonic tombs (including Tutankhamun's) contained coriander seeds, and it is mentioned in the Book of Exodus as resembling manna.

Ancient Greeks and Romans used the seeds for flavoring and medicine. The plant has a unique global cultural split: in most Anglosphere usage "coriander" means the seed and "cilantro" (Spanish for coriander) means the fresh leaf, reflecting the Americas' stronger connection to Mexican cuisine. Indian "dhania" covers both.

A substantial genetic polymorphism in the human OR6A2 olfactory receptor gene causes a significant minority of people to perceive cilantro leaf as tasting like soap — a trait concentrated in European-heritage populations and largely absent in populations with long cilantro-eating traditions. Essential to Mexican, Indian, Thai, Vietnamese, and Middle Eastern cuisines. The 'cilantro soap gene' (OR6A2) was identified in 2012 — carriers detect aldehyde compounds in the leaves that others perceive as fresh and citrusy. This genetic divide has created one of food's most passionate debates. In Thai cuisine, the root (not just leaves or seeds) is a crucial paste ingredient. Coriander seed was an ingredient in the original Coca-Cola recipe. India is the world's largest producer and consumer.
name_origin: Coriandrum from Greek 'koris' (bedbug) — the fresh leaves' smell was compared to crushed bedbugs. Sativum means 'cultivated.'

uses_list.text: Fresh cilantro leaves and dried Coriander seeds flavor world cuisines
Lacy white umbels attract hoverflies and beneficial wasps

symbolism_list.description: Named for bugs, dividing humanity genetically — it hides complexity beneath simplicity

symbolism_story: Coriander is concealment in herb form — its name comes from the Greek koris, bedbug, for the divisive scent of it leaves, and a single gene splits humanity into those who taste cilantro as bright citrus and those who taste soap. Beneath its plain feathery foliage hides this quiet genetic drama. It is the herb that reminds us our perceptions of even small things are not as shared as we assume.

fragrance.notes: The flowers have a mild scent.

bloom_tip: White flat flower clusters May to June
fruit_tip: Blue-black berries on red stems August

description: Pagoda Dogwood is a beautiful native American small tree of the eastern United States, distinguished by its horizontally tiered branches that give it the appearance of a pagoda or wedding cake. Growing 15-25 feet tall, it bears flat clusters of small white flowers in late spring followed by blue-black berries on red stems and burgundy fall foliage. A refined specimen for American woodland edges in USDA zones 3-7.
history_text_short: Pagoda dogwood is native to eastern North America from Newfoundland to Georgia. Described by Linnaeus's son in 1782, its distinctive tiered horizontal branching inspired the pagoda common name and made it a signature tree of American native woodland plantings.
history_text_long:
Cornus alternifolia is native to moist woodland edges and forest openings across eastern North America from Newfoundland through Ontario south to northern Georgia and west to Minnesota. Carl Linnaeus the Younger formally described it in 1782, noting its unusual alternate leaf arrangement—most Cornus species have opposite leaves. Its horizontal tiered branching creates elegant layered silhouettes earning the common name pagoda dogwood.

Indigenous peoples including the Menominee used bark and root decoctions for medicinal purposes. The cultivar 'Argentea' with variegated white-edged leaves, introduced in the 19th century, remains widely grown. Plantsman Michael Dirr and others championed it in the late 20th century American native plant movement.

Unfortunately Cornus golden canker (Cryptodiaporthe) has caused problems in some regions. Unlike most dogwoods, its leaves are alternate rather than opposite, giving it its botanical name. The cultivar 'Golden Shadows' with yellow-variegated foliage became a Proven Winners sensation in American gardens in the 2000s.
name_origin: 'Alternifolia' refers to the alternate leaf arrangement, unusual among Cornus species.

uses_list.text: Tiered horizontal branching gives pagoda-like silhouette
Blue-black drupes feed thrushes and woodland songbirds
Native small tree for shaded woodland-edge plantings

symbolism_list.description: horizontal tiered form evokes Japanese gardens
refined architectural beauty

symbolism_story: The Alternate-Leaved Dogwood holds Serenity in its tiered, horizontal branching — a form so reminiscent of Japanese garden design it is often called the pagoda dogwood. Each layer offers a quiet study in grace, architecture as much as botany. Even leafless in winter, its silhouette teaches the eye how stillness is composed.

fragrance.notes: The flowers have a mild scent.

bloom_tip: Creamy-white clusters May to June
fruit_tip: Blue-black berries in late summer
